# Trichy Assault Rifle

The Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) is an officially designated Indian assault rifle chambered in 7.62×39mm, developed between 2011 and 2015 . It is not a colloquialism but a formal model name recognizing the role of its primary developer and manufacturer, the Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) , . The rifle entered service in 2017 and remains in active production and use as of May 2025 . Conceived as an AK-47 equivalent, the TAR was designed to offer enhanced reliability in adverse conditions for India's Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs), State Police forces, and paramilitary units , . Its successful adoption across multiple security agencies highlights its significance as a key component of India's efforts to modernize its internal security arsenal while pursuing long-term self-reliance in defense manufacturing. The weapon system is characterized by its robust, gas-operated action, selectable single-shot and burst-fire modes, and a versatile family of variants including fixed-stock, side-folding, down-folding, and carbine configurations , .

## Development and Design

The development of the Trichy Assault Rifle was undertaken by the Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT), a state-owned enterprise established in Tiruchirappalli, Tamil Nadu, in 1966 . OFT operates under the administrative control of the Ordnance Factories Board, which itself falls under the Ministry of Defence of the Government of India . The factory began its production activities in 1967 and has since been responsible for manufacturing various automatic rifles, including the INSAS and the 1A1 . The genesis of the TAR project occurred in the early 2010s, with some sources indicating the initial development phase spanned from 2011 to 2015, while others place the start date at 2015 , . The rifle was officially christened and unveiled around 2013 during OFT Day celebrations, where it was presented as a significant achievement for the factory . This formal designation distinguishes it from informal descriptors used in media and reports, such as "AKM-based rifle" or "AK-47-derived assault rifle," which accurately describe its lineage but do not reflect its official nomenclature , .

The design philosophy behind the Trichy Assault Rifle was rooted in creating a reliable, cost-effective, and domestically produced stop-gap solution to equip the vast number of personnel in India's paramilitary and police forces . The strategic goal was to provide a capable replacement for aging weapons systems over the subsequent decade, particularly for counter-insurgency (COIN) operations conducted by units such as the Rashtriya Rifles, J&K SOG, and COBRA . By leveraging the proven and battle-tested design principles of the AK platform, specifically the AKM, OFT aimed to produce a weapon that would be resilient to the harsh environmental conditions often encountered during internal security duties , . This approach prioritized mechanical simplicity and durability, core tenets of the original AK design, while incorporating modern features requested by users. Key indigenous design elements include a machined mono-block receiver body, which enhances structural integrity and precision, and fibre-reinforced polymer magazines with steel inserts, balancing weight reduction with robustness , .

The developmental process included critical user trials to validate the rifle's performance before full-scale induction. These trials, conducted at locations such as the CRPF Academy in Kadarpur, Haryana, involved extensive testing to ensure reliability and effectiveness , . A pivotal moment in the TAR's development was the successful completion of these field trials in November 2017, during which 15,000 rounds were fired without a single stoppage, demonstrating exceptional reliability , . This success was instrumental in securing procurement orders from various security agencies. The General Manager of OFT, M. K. Mishra, had stated upon the rifle's unveiling that it was expected to become a "pride of India" once adopted by the armed forces and security agencies . Another General Manager, Shirish Khare, later described the TAR as the factory's most significant weapons development success in the preceding 12–13 years, underscoring its importance within the Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli's portfolio . The rifle's development aligns with India's broader national strategy to reduce reliance on foreign imports and bolster domestic manufacturing capabilities through initiatives like 'Make in India'. The TAR stands as a testament to the potential of India's public sector undertakings to deliver sophisticated and effective defense equipment tailored to the nation's specific operational requirements.

## Technical Specifications

The Trichy Assault Rifle is a selective-fire weapon designed for versatility and reliability in diverse operational environments. Its core technical specifications are centered around the 7.62×39mm intermediate cartridge, a round known for its balance of power and controllability, widely used in Kalashnikov-pattern rifles , . The rifle employs a gas-operated reloading mechanism, a hallmark of the AK platform, which contributes to its renowned dependability , . The overall mass of the standard Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) variant is approximately 3.4 kg when unloaded, making it a manageable weapon for infantry personnel , . Its overall length is 900 mm, providing a balanced profile suitable for general-purpose combat scenarios , . The barrel length measures 650 mm, which is crucial for achieving optimal muzzle velocity and accuracy .

In terms of performance, the TAR is capable of a rate of fire of 600 rounds per minute in full-automatic mode . The muzzle velocity of the 7.62×39mm ammunition is recorded between 710–715 m/s, delivering sufficient energy for effective engagement at medium ranges . The effective firing range for the standard TAR is cited as being between 300–350 meters, though some sources extend the aimed fire range up to 500 meters, with a destructive effect extending to 1350 meters , , . This indicates its capability for both precise target engagement and suppressive fire. The weapon utilizes a feed system consisting of 30-round detachable box magazines, which are supplied by Nilkamal Limited . The design incorporates a Picatinny rail, allowing for the attachment of various optical sights and scopes to adapt to different mission profiles , .

| Specification | Value | Source(s) |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| **Caliber** | 7.62×39mm | , , |
| **Action** | Gas-operated reloading | , , |
| **Feed System** | 30-round detachable box magazine | |
| **Rate of Fire** | 600 rounds/min (full auto) | |
| **Muzzle Velocity** | 710–715 m/s | |
| **Effective Range** | 300–350 m (standard TAR); Up to 500 m (aimed fire) | , , , |
| **Overall Length** | 900 mm (butt open) | , , |
| **Barrel Length** | 650 mm | |

| **Magazine Material** | Fibre-reinforced polymer with steel inserts | , |

This comprehensive set of specifications underscores the TAR's design as a modernized, reliable, and adaptable infantry weapon, engineered to meet the demanding needs of India's security forces.

## Variants and Accessories

The Trichy Assault Rifle program has evolved beyond a single model, producing a versatile family of variants to address a wide spectrum of operational requirements. This modular approach allows different branches of India's security apparatus to select the configuration best suited to their specific missions, whether for general patrol duties, vehicle crew protection, or specialized counter-terrorism operations. The primary variants include the standard fixed-stock version, alongside several folding stock iterations designed to enhance portability and maneuverability in confined spaces. The Side-Folding Butt Version was launched on August 25, 2021, commemorating 75 years of Indian independence, and is specifically produced for CAPF units to support mobility during guard and patrolling duties . Similarly, the Down Folding Butt Version offers the same benefits of compactness when folded, with an overall length of 900 mm when extended and 650 mm when folded , . In addition to these folding models, a TriCa carbine was unveiled in January 2021, offering a shorter-barreled option for increased portability .

Perhaps the most innovative development within the TAR family is the TAR-3 "Baby TAR." This compact, unsolicited in-house innovation was developed by OFT to solve the inherent challenges of short-barrel firearms, such as excessive heat generation, flash, and noise . The TAR-3 features an 8.3-inch barrel, an overall length of 19.2 inches when the stock is folded, and weighs just 2.7 kg, making it significantly lighter than a standard AK-47 . To mitigate the thermal issues of its short barrel, OFT incorporated indigenously designed solutions, including internal metal reflectors to insulate the foregrip and a compact flash hider, which together enable sustained fire of approximately 120 rounds (four full magazines) without overheating . During unofficial Indian Army trials, three prototypes each fired over 2,000 rounds consecutively without a stoppage, showcasing remarkable reliability for such a compact design . The TAR-3 was intended for special forces, counter-terror operators, and crews of aircraft, tanks, and other vehicles, highlighting OFT's ability to innovate rapidly based on practical battlefield experience .

The TAR platform is also highly adaptable due to its extensive accessory ecosystem. It is compatible with Under-Barrel Grenade Launchers (UBGLs) of the 40x46mm caliber, including the GP-25, GP-30, and Arsenal M6, which can be mounted via the proprietary UBGL interface , , . The rifle is equipped with a monoblock receiver and shockproof polymer lower parts, ensuring durability under stress . Furthermore, the inclusion of two Picatinny rails—one on the handguard and one on the top cover—allows for the flexible mounting of a wide array of optics, laser sights, and tactical lights, enabling operators to customize their weapon system according to mission-specific needs . This combination of varied physical configurations and advanced accessories makes the Trichy Assault Rifle a highly flexible and potent weapon system for a multitude of security and combat scenarios.

## Adoption and Deployment

Following successful user trials that demonstrated high reliability, the Trichy Assault Rifle achieved rapid and widespread adoption across India's security architecture , . The first deliveries were made to the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), a premier Central Armed Police Force (CAPF), with an initial batch of 500 units delivered on March 13, 2020 , . This initial procurement was part of a larger order for 6,167 rifles, signaling the CRPF's confidence in the new weapon , . The success with the CRPF paved the way for broader procurement across other CAPFs and state police forces. By March 2021, OFT had supplied over 11,500 TAR units to various CAPFs, and as of December 2020, more than 10,000 rifles had already been delivered to police forces including the Chhattisgarh Police, Border Security Force (BSF), and Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) , , . The BSF, another major CAPF, announced a limited procurement of 125 additional TAR units in January 2024, this time equipped with bayonets and other essential accessories , .

Beyond the CAPFs, the Indian Army has also procured the Trichy Assault Rifle, albeit in a more measured fashion. During the 2020–21 fiscal year, OFT manufactured and dispatched over 11,000 TAR rifles valued at ₹160 crore to meet Indian Army requirements . While the exact extent of its deployment within regular Army infantry brigades is less specified compared to its use by paramilitary forces, this procurement confirms its acceptance as a viable infantry weapon for the country's main fighting force. The adoption by the Army is part of a broader effort to replace the aging Indian Small Arms System (INSAS) rifles, for which the TAR serves as a contemporary, AK-pattern alternative . The rifle's suitability for counter-insurgency and counter-terrorism operations, combined with its proven reliability, has made it a preferred choice for units engaged in internal security duties, where operational environments can be unpredictable and unforgiving , .

The deployment timeline of the TAR reflects a strategic rollout to equip India's security apparatus with a modern, reliable, and domestically produced infantry weapon. The table below summarizes the key procurement and delivery milestones for the Trichy Assault Rifle.

| Agency/Force | Procurement Date(s) | Quantity Supplied / Announced | Source(s) |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| **Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF)** | March 2020 (Initial Batch) | 500 units delivered | , |
| **Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF)** | Not Specified | Part of a total order of 6,167 rifles | , |
| **Various Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs)** | By March 2021 | Over 11,500 units supplied | |
| **Chhattisgarh Police** | By December 2020 | Over 10,000 units supplied | , , |
| **Border Security Force (BSF)** | December 2020 | More than 10,000 units delivered | |
| **Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP)** | December 2020 | More than 10,000 units delivered | , , |
| **Indian Army** | 2020–21 Fiscal Year | Over 11,000 units manufactured and dispatched | |
| **Border Security Force (BSF)** | January 15, 2024 | Additional procurement of 125 units | , |

This systematic and multi-agency adoption underscores the TAR's integral role in enhancing the combat capability of India's security forces.

## Comparative Analysis and Strategic Context

The Trichy Assault Rifle exists within a complex landscape of indigenous Indian small arms development, necessitating clear differentiation from other prominent platforms like the INSAS and Excalibur rifles. While all are products of India's push for self-reliance, they represent distinct design philosophies, calibers, and operational roles. The most direct comparison is with the INSAS (Indian National Small Arms System), which is an indigenous design featuring a bullpup configuration and primarily chambered in the 5.56×45mm NATO cartridge , . In contrast, the TAR is an AK-pattern rifle, utilizing the 7.62×39mm intermediate cartridge, which provides greater stopping power at closer ranges typical of COIN operations , . The TAR was conceived not as a wholesale replacement for the INSAS in the Indian Army, but rather as a complementary system filling a specific niche, particularly for the CAPFs and state police who require a weapon that balances power, reliability, and manageability , .

A more pointed comparison can be drawn with the Excalibur rifle. Both the TAR and Excalibur were developed by the Ordnance Factories Board (OFB) and DRDO's Armament Research and Development Establishment (ARDE), but they are fundamentally different designs . The Excalibur is a 5.56×45mm rifle derived from the INSAS platform, whereas the TAR is a 7.62×39mm rifle based on the AKM , , . Their post-trial trajectories diverged dramatically. Despite passing initial user trials in 2014-15, the Excalibur ultimately failed final army tests in June 2017 due to deficiencies in quality control and firepower , . Consequently, the Indian Army rejected it for standard issue, although it was certified for interim use pending the outcome of a new multi-calibre rifle tender , . The Excalibur's troubled history led to its rejection by the Indian Armed Forces and major CAPFs, despite being procured in limited numbers by several state police forces . Conversely, the Trichy Assault Rifle successfully navigated its own user trials, leading to large-scale procurement by the CRPF, BSF, ITBP, and even the Indian Army , . This stark contrast illustrates the variability in outcomes of India's defense modernization programs, positioning the TAR as a pragmatic and successful execution of a proven design philosophy, while the Excalibur represents a case study in the challenges of adapting and upgrading existing indigenous platforms.

Strategically, the TAR fits into India's broader objective of achieving self-reliance in defense manufacturing, encapsulated by the 'Atmanirbhar Bharat' (Self-reliant India) initiative. However, its role is nuanced. It serves as a bridge solution—a reliable, readily available, and cost-effective weapon that modernizes the arsenals of India's internal security forces while the country simultaneously pursues more ambitious, cutting-edge indigenous programs , . The most significant of these next-generation projects is the Ugram assault rifle. Developed by DRDO's ARDE in collaboration with private industry, the Ugram is a fully indigenous 7.62×51mm NATO caliber weapon designed to meet the stringent General Staff Qualitative Requirements (GSQRs) for the Indian Armed Forces , . The Ugram program aims to provide a technologically superior alternative to the aging INSAS rifles and to serve as the definitive infantry weapon for the future . The relationship between the TAR and the Ugram is therefore one of complementarity and succession. The TAR provides immediate capability enhancement and fills a gap left by the complexities of developing entirely new systems. The Ugram, once fully developed, tested, and fielded, is intended to be the long-term replacement for both the INSAS and potentially the TAR, representing the pinnacle of India's indigenous small arms technology , . The TAR, therefore, is not merely another rifle but a critical piece of India's dual-track strategy: leveraging proven, accessible designs for immediate needs while investing heavily in R&D for future dominance.

## Production Status and Future Outlook

As of May 2025, the Trichy Assault Rifle remains in active production and continues to be a vital asset for India's security forces . The Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli, the sole manufacturer, has demonstrated a consistent capacity for mass production, having fulfilled large-scale orders for the Indian Army, CAPFs, and state police forces over several years , . The ongoing production ensures that the TAR will remain a staple of India's internal security apparatus for the foreseeable future, providing a reliable and potent infantry weapon system. The rifle's continued relevance is underscored by the development of new variants like the TAR-3 "Baby TAR," which showcases OFT's innovative capabilities and commitment to meeting evolving operational demands . This continuous development pipeline suggests that the TAR platform is not static but is being actively adapted to new threats and mission sets, thereby extending its service life and utility.

The future outlook for the Trichy Assault Rifle is intrinsically linked to the development and eventual induction of next-generation indigenous rifles, most notably the Ugram assault rifle. The Ugram program represents a significant technological leap, aiming to replace the aging INSAS system with a state-of-the-art weapon that meets the highest international standards , . Comprehensive user trials for the Ugram were conducted in May 2024 involving multiple CAPFs, with positive feedback received regarding its accuracy, reliability, and handling . The NSG, a premier counter-terrorism unit, plans a limited initial procurement of the Ugram following these trials, paving the way for wider fielding . As the Ugram matures and begins to enter service in larger quantities, the role of the TAR may gradually shift. It could transition from a frontline infantry weapon in some capacities to a dedicated system for specialized units or continue to serve as a robust workhorse for general-purpose duties within the CAPFs and state police.

In conclusion, the Trichy Assault Rifle stands as a significant achievement in India's journey toward defense self-reliance. It was successfully conceived, developed, and fielded to meet a pressing need for a reliable and effective infantry weapon for the country's internal security forces. Its adoption by the CRPF, BSF, ITBP, and the Indian Army validates its design and performance , . While it is not a permanent fixture and is likely destined to be superseded by more advanced platforms like the Ugram, the TAR has served its purpose admirably as a bridge solution , . It provided a stable, proven, and domestically produced capability that allowed India to modernize its security forces without relying on foreign suppliers. For now, the Trichy Assault Rifle remains a cornerstone of India's small arms inventory, a testament to the engineering prowess of its public sector and its indispensable role in safeguarding the nation's internal security.

As of May 2025, the Trichy Assault Rifle remains in active production and continues to be a vital asset for India's security forces.

The Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli, the sole manufacturer, has demonstrated a consistent capacity for mass production, having fulfilled large-scale orders for the Indian Army, CAPFs, and state police forces over several years.
The ongoing production ensures that the TAR will remain a staple of India's internal security apparatus for the foreseeable future, providing a reliable and potent infantry weapon system.

The rifle's continued relevance is underscored by the development of new variants like the TAR-3 "Baby TAR," which showcases OFT's innovative capabilities and commitment to meeting evolving operational demands.
This continuous development pipeline suggests that the TAR platform is not static but is being actively adapted to new threats and mission sets, thereby extending its service life and utility.
The future outlook for the Trichy Assault Rifle is intrinsically linked to the development and eventual induction of next-generation indigenous rifles, most notably the Ugram assault rifle.
The Ugram program represents a significant technological leap, aiming to replace the aging INSAS system with a state-of-the-art weapon that meets the highest international standards.
Comprehensive user trials for the Ugram were conducted in May 2024 involving multiple CAPFs, with positive feedback received regarding its accuracy, reliability, and handling.
The NSG, a premier counter-terrorism unit, plans a limited initial procurement of the Ugram following these trials, paving the way for wider fielding.
As the Ugram matures and begins to enter service in larger quantities, the role of the TAR may gradually shift.

The TAR could transition from a frontline infantry weapon in some capacities to a dedicated system for specialized units or continue to serve as a robust workhorse for general-purpose duties within the CAPFs and state police.
The Trichy Assault Rifle stands as a significant achievement in India's journey toward defense self-reliance.
The TAR was successfully conceived, developed, and fielded to meet a pressing need for a reliable and effective infantry weapon for the country's internal security forces.
Its adoption by the CRPF, BSF, ITBP, and the Indian Army validates its design and performance.
While it is not a permanent fixture and is likely destined to be superseded by more advanced platforms like the Ugram, the TAR has served its purpose admirably as a bridge solution.
The TAR provided a stable, proven, and domestically produced capability that allowed India to modernize its security forces without relying on foreign suppliers.

For now, the Trichy Assault Rifle remains a cornerstone of India's small arms inventory, a testament to the engineering prowess of its public sector and its indispensable role in safeguarding the nation's internal security.

BSF To Procure More Made-In-India Trichy Assault Rifles
=======================================================

BSF To Procure More Made-In-India Trichy Assault Rifles

Monday, January 15, 2024 by [Indian Defence News](https://www.blogger.com/profile/10039798451461108617)


==================================================================================================================================================================

![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjR_6KQW-dlRmJMFDgkmJHvIN6zxHHRz5SCWtwdpwIofRbn7S_6-PzX_cjkFy-Avno7sfNWct0lxVm8lRexBNOb7fRJVXpxtsvP6LGQI0GJPlA9ZiXQ25gYOts4kOHXAZ8rhyJ8xPms7zLIbNnKoaPVR_ApisaikLnKsTCB_20EZB-yBvfvin85iwJrk1E/s16000/Trichy_Assault_Rifle.jpg)

  

_BSF plans to arm its personnel with the 125 more indigenous Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), with bayonets and accessories in a limited procurement_

  

**New Delhi:** The Border Security Force (BSF) is gearing up to equip its personnel with the Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), an indigenously developed firearm, according to an official statement. The procurement is set at a limited quantity, with the BSF acquiring 125 rifles along with bayonets and other accessory items.

  

TAR: Firepower Tailored For Specialised Needs of Paramilitary

  

The primary objective behind this move is to set an example for other wings of the Armed Forces and Paramilitary, encouraging them to follow suit and procure more indigenous arms. The initiative aims to strengthen India's self-sufficiency in defence capabilities.

  

“Ordnance Factory, Trichirappalli developed and manufactured TAR Down folding butt version to meet the customer requirement as some of the CAPF units, State Police and RPF required the Down folding butt version for quick and easy movement of personnel in guard and patrolling duty”, said Officials in a prior statement.

  

Trichy Assault Rifle: Counter-Terror Operations with Cutting-Edge Firepower

  

> _1\. The TAR, chambered in 7.62x39mm, has a lightweight modular design, making it well-suited for counter-insurgency and counter-terror operations._
> 
> _2\. Its gas-operated mechanism, machined mono-block receiver body, and fibre-reinforced polymer magazine with steel inserts contribute to its effectiveness in the field._
> 
> _3\. The rifle operates in both single-shot and burst modes, with the latter capable of destroying targets at a range of up to 500m. The TAR's overall destructive range extends to 1350m._
> 
> _4\. A customised version featuring a single-round firing mode is designed specifically for police forces engaged in patrolling duties within urban areas. The TAR-Down folding butt has an overall length of 900mm in the butt-open condition and 650mm in the butt-folding condition._
> 
> _5\. The rifle's versatility is further increased with the option to fit a 40x46mm UBGL GP-25, GP-30, and M6, catering to various operational requirements. Additionally, the inclusion of Tritium-filled sources for night firing and a Picatinny rail for mounting optical sights underlines the rifle’s adaptability to diverse scenarios._

  

In 2020, the Ordnance Factory of Tiruchirappalli (OFT) delivered the initial batch of 500 Trichy Assault Rifles (TAR) to the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), fulfilling a total order of 6,167 assault rifles.

  

The procurement followed rigorous field trials, including evaluation sessions at the CRPF Academy in Kadarpur, Haryana, in November 2017. Testing focused on the TAR's functionality, accuracy, and reliability, with 15,000 rounds fired without a single stoppage, affirming the weapon's dependability.

  

OFT has further supplied over 10,000 rifles to Chhattisgarh police and various central armed reserve police forces, including the ITBP, BSF, and CISF. Shirish Khare, OFT's General Manager had proudly acclaimed the Trichy Assault Rifle as their most significant success in the past 12-13 years of weapons development.

  

With a focus on promoting indigenous weaponry, the adoption of the TAR by the BSF signifies an important step in fortifying the nation's Paramilitary security apparatus. This move aligns with broader initiatives to reduce dependence on foreign arms, fostering self-sufficiency in defence production.

Special Service and Features
Launch of 7.62*39mm Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) Down Folding Butt Version
प्रविष्टि तिथि: 26 AUG 2021 12:51PM by PIB Chennai

In commemoration of 75 years of independence, Ordnance Factory, Tiruchirappalli launched Down folding butt version of 7.62*39mm Trichy Assault Rifle on 25th August 2021.  At present, Ordnance Factory, Tiruchirappali, is manufacturing TAR Rifles in two variants i.e. Fixed butt and side folding butt versions.

    The 7.62*39mm Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) is a powerful individual automatic weapon designed to destroy the enemy by fire in single and burst firing mode.  It is a single shot Rifle in normal mode and it can be used in burst mode also.  By firing in burst mode in short series, group or single targets at a range up to 500m can be destroyed.  However, the destructive effect of the TAR is up to a range of 1350m.

          Ordnance Factory, Trichirappallin developed and manufactured TAR  Down folding butt version to meet the customer requirement as some of the CAPF units, State Police and RPF required the Down folding butt version for quick and easy movement of personnel in guard and patrolling duty.

  The overall length of TAR-Down folding butt is 900mm in butt open condition and 650mm in butt folding condition.

 The Down folding butt version of 7.62*39mm Trichy Assault Rifle launched by Shri Sanjay Dwivedi, IOFS, General Manager, Ordnance Factory, Trichirappalli and Shri Rajiv Jain, IOFS, Addl. General Manager, Shri A.K.Singh, IOFS, Addl.General Manager Shri V. Gunasekaran, IOFS, Joint General Manager, Shri S. Krishanaswamy, IOFS, Joint General Manager and other Officers of OFT attended the function.

The **Trichy assault rifle** (TAR), sometimes known as the **Tiruchi assault rifle**,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3) is an [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India")\-made [assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle "Assault rifle") chambered for the [7.62×39mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7.62%C3%9739mm "7.62×39mm") round. The TAR is based on the [AR-M1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1 "AR-M1"), produced by [Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria") manufacturer [Arsenal AD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_AD "Arsenal AD"). Developed between 2011 and 2015, [Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli "Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli") (OFT) began manufacturing TARs in 2017.

The TAR was developed to reduce dependence on [imported](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Import "Import") AR-M1s under the [Atmanirbhar Bharat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmanirbhar_Bharat "Atmanirbhar Bharat") self-reliance policy. The TAR has been adopted by most [Indian law enforcement agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement_in_India "Law enforcement in India").

Prior to the TAR's introduction, India largely used foreign-made [AK-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalashnikov_rifle "Kalashnikov rifle") rifles. Around 500,000 M1s were reportedly imported by India from Bulgaria in 2021 for use by the [Central Armed Police Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Armed_Police_Forces "Central Armed Police Forces") (CAPF) and [Indian police forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Police_Service "Indian Police Service").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4) As of May 2025, India is the [second-largest arms importer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_industry#World's_largest_arms_importers "Arms industry") after [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine"), accounting for 8.3% of the arms trade, according to research data from the [Stockholm International Peace Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_International_Peace_Research_Institute "Stockholm International Peace Research Institute").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-5) To reduce dependence on importing small arms from other countries, part of the [Atmanirbhar Bharat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmanirbhar_Bharat "Atmanirbhar Bharat") policy called for self-sufficiency to manufacture firearms in India.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-6)

OFT announced the manufacture of an indigenous AK-based assault rifle in 2011.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-oldnew-8) The AR was named Trichy after OFT to recognise the factory's contribution in developing and manufacturing the rifle.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-9) Some TARs were made in 2012 to be tested.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10) These early TARs were tested by the [Border Security Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security_Force "Border Security Force") (BSF), the [Central Reserve Police Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Reserve_Police_Force "Central Reserve Police Force") (CRPF), the [Indo-Tibetan Border Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Tibetan_Border_Police "Indo-Tibetan Border Police") and the [Sashastra Seema Bal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sashastra_Seema_Bal "Sashastra Seema Bal").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10)

Development started in 2015[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11) with a production line established in 2017.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-13) That March, 200 TARs were acquired by the [Chhattisgarh Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chhattisgarh_Police "Chhattisgarh Police")[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TrichyF-14) as part of the 216th Ordnance Factories Day celebration.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15) Concerns were raised at the time, prior to manufacture, that OFT was experiencing manpower decline, leading to a decline of employees at the company.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THA-16) The [All India Defence Employees Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_India_Defence_Employees_Federation "All India Defence Employees Federation"), the [Indian National Defence Workers' Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Defence_Workers%27_Federation "Indian National Defence Workers' Federation"), and the [Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharatiya_Pratiraksha_Mazdoor_Sangh "Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh") stated their opposition to importing small arms with the unions hoping that more orders for the TAR would be approved, retaining employees at OFT.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THA-16)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg/250px-Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg)

A [CISF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Industrial_Security_Force "Central Industrial Security Force") officer practices with the TAR at a shooting range.

In November 2017, the CRPF conducted field tests to determine the suitability of the TAR with 15,000 rounds fired[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12) at the [CRPF Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRPF_Academy "CRPF Academy") in Kadarpur, [Haryana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haryana "Haryana") with no reports of the rifle jamming.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-17) Other tests conducted included the TAR being fired from mud, rain and saltwater and from being dropped to test reliability and accuracy.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) 100 TARs were ordered afterwards.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) In February 2018, further tests were conducted by the CRPF at Jagdalpur, Raipur, Guwahati and Srinagar with an order of 6,167 TARs placed afterwards.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12) At the time, the CRPF tested the Trichy with the Ghatak, the [Joint Venture Protective Carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Venture_Protective_Carbine "Joint Venture Protective Carbine") and the [INSAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INSAS_rifle "INSAS rifle")1C.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-19) In March 2020, the CRPF acquired the first 500 out of 6,167 TARs sold to them.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11)

In January 2019, the TAR was delivered to the BSF, with its Additional Director General Nasir Kamal receiving the first rifle from the [Ordnance Factory Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directorate_of_Ordnance_/(Coordination_%26_Services/) "Directorate of Ordnance (Coordination & Services)")'s Director General Saurabh Kumar.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3) It was reported in the same month that the [Jharkhand Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jharkhand_Police "Jharkhand Police") would acquire TARs for anti-Naxalite operations.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-JPR-20) The TAR was displayed for the first time at the Pragati Maidan in [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi") for the 5th International Police Expo and the 4th India Homeland Security Expo.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-21) In February 2020, the TAR was on public display at the Defence Expo at [Lucknow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucknow "Lucknow"), [Uttar Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttar_Pradesh "Uttar Pradesh").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22) It was reported at the time that the TAR was offered to the [Indian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Army "Indian Army").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22) OFT reported in March 2021 that around 11,500 TARs were supplied for a total of [Rs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupee_sign "Rupee sign") 1.60 billion during fiscal year 2020–21.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-23)

In January 2021, the TriCa (Trichy Carbine) Carbine was unveiled.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) Tests were conducted where 2,000 rounds were fired with no stoppages.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4) That August, OFT announced that the TAR could use the [ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARDE_Under_Barrel_Grenade_Launcher "ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher"), which was presented by OFT general manager Sanjay Dwivedi.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-UBGL-24) A TAR variant with a downfolding stock was presented publicly.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-PR-25) This variant was sought out by the [Railway Protection Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_Protection_Force "Railway Protection Force") aside from the CAPFs.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-26) In December 2021, the [National Security Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Guard "National Security Guard") placed an order of 100 TriCa carbines.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NSGTriCa-27) On April 2022, the [Kerala Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_Police "Kerala Police") (KP) ordered 92 TriCa carbines.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPTriCa-28) According to OFT, the [Greyhounds unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhounds_/(police/) "Greyhounds (police)") ordered 44 TARs.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPTriCa-28) In July 2022, the [Government of Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Kerala "Government of Kerala") received a request from KP to procure 250 TARs with side folding stocks;[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-29) they received the TriCa carbines in May 2025.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPH-30) According to the [Advanced Weapons and Equipment India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India "Advanced Weapons and Equipment India")'s (AWEIL) 2022–2023 Annual Report, the [National Security Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Guard "National Security Guard") and the [Andhra Pradesh Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andhra_Pradesh_Police "Andhra Pradesh Police") conducted tests on both the TAR and the TriCa carbine.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-31)

In January 2023, the [Central Industrial Security Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Industrial_Security_Force "Central Industrial Security Force") (CISF) received TARs manufactured from [Rifle Factory Ishapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifle_Factory_Ishapore "Rifle Factory Ishapore").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-32) That April, Minister of State for Defence and Tourism [Ajay Bhatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajay_Bhatt_/(politician/) "Ajay Bhatt (politician)") visited OFT, where he witnessed the TAR being manufactured in the factory while briefed on OFT's research and development work.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-33) The following January, BSF procured further TARs featuring bayonets.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Bayonet-34) The Government of Kerala published an approved plan for the KP to acquire 30 TARs.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-35) In November 2023, the Trichy was on display at the Dasara Exhibition in [Mysore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysore "Mysore"), [Karnataka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnataka "Karnataka") as part of an effort to raise awareness on crime and public safety.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-36) In a July 2024 interview with Rajesh Choudhary, Chairman and Managing Director of AWEIL, he said that the TAR continues to be in demand with CAPFs and reported that an export order was made for the rifle.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-AWEILI-37) In May 2025, it was reported that the Assam Forest Department and the [Central Bureau of Narcotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bureau_of_Narcotics "Central Bureau of Narcotics") made orders for the TriCa carbine.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPH-30)

Initial versions of the TAR were produced by using [FN FAL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FN_FAL "FN FAL")\-based receivers and were using 7.62x39 mm magazines.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-oldnew-8) In 2012, there were reports that the prototypes jammed during testing due to the rate of fire being 800 rounds per minutes instead of 600 rounds per minute to match with the AK-47.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10) It was initially expected that the rate of fire would be at 650 rounds per minute.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10)

The current version of the TAR is based on the AR-M1[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-38) with a machined receiver instead of stamped sheet to ensure the rifle has high accuracy and reliability.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) The TAR can be outfitted with [picatinny rails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picatinny_rail "Picatinny rail") on the upper handguard to attach scopes if requested.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18)

In July 2021, it was reported that the TARs used by the [Kerala Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_Police "Kerala Police") are effective in [Naxalite-Maoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naxalite%E2%80%93Maoist_insurgency "Naxalite–Maoist insurgency") [counterinsurgency operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterinsurgency "Counterinsurgency").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-39)

On August 2025, a TAR was secured from pro-Maoist communist [Naxalite fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Guerrilla_Army_/(India/) "People's Liberation Guerrilla Army (India)") in Chhattisgarh’s [Narayanpur district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narayanpur_district "Narayanpur district").[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-cp-40)

The TAR can fire with single, burst and full automatic mode.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TrichyDemand-41) OFT reported that the TAR can be adopted with single shot mode only for police forces in cities and urban areas.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-OFTTR-1) While it has an effective range of 300 to 350 metres,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-AWEIL2122-42) the range can be up to 500 metres if the rifle is used in full auto.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15)

OFT claimed that the TAR is functionally on par with the AK-47.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22)

The TAR can be equipped with several [underbarrel grenade launchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenade_launcher "Grenade launcher"), including the [ARDE UBGL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARDE_Under_Barrel_Grenade_Launcher "ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher"),[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-43) the [GP-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GP-25 "GP-25"), the GP-30 and the Arsenal M6 UBGL.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11) The TAR can use bayonets.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Bayonet-34)

[Magazines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine_/(firearms/) "Magazine (firearms)") for the TAR are supplied by Nilkamal Limited.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-44) Magazines made for [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47")\-based assault rifles can also be used.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-na-45)

[7.62×39 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7.62%C3%9739_mm "7.62×39 mm") ammunition of all types can be used for the TAR.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-na-45)

[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Trichy_AR_actual_model.jpg/330px-Trichy_AR_actual_model.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trichy_AR_actual_model.jpg)

[![Image 5](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e2/TAR_folding_stock_models.jpg/330px-TAR_folding_stock_models.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TAR_folding_stock_models.jpg)

[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/48/TriCa_carbine_with_folded_stock.jpg/330px-TriCa_carbine_with_folded_stock.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TriCa_carbine_with_folded_stock.jpg)

TAR variants. From top to bottom: TAR side folding stock, TAR down folding stock and TriCa carbine.

### Trichy assault rifle

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Trichy assault rifle")\]

Main variant with a fixed stock.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3)

### Trichy folding stock (side)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Trichy folding stock (side)")\]

TAR variant with a side folding stock.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3)

### Trichy folding stock (down)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Trichy folding stock (down)")\]

Unveiled on August 2021, it is a TAR variant with a downfolding stock.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-PR-25)

It's sometimes referred to as a variant with an underfolding stock.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4)

### Trichy Carbine (TriCa)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Trichy Carbine (TriCa)")\]

Unveiled on January 2021, the TriCa weights 3.17 kg and is marketed as a compact weapon for vehicle crews, paratroopers and special forces units.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) The TriCA's firing range is from 150-175 metres.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) A muzzle device is installed on the barrel to minimize muzzle flash and sound when it's fired.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2)

The TriCa is a clone based on the Arsenal AR-M14SF, but the muzzle device is based on the AKS-74U.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-47)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-MILMAG-46)

It is sometimes known as **Baby TAR** or **TAR-3**.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4)
