Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) is a government-owned small arms manufacturing facility located in [Tiruchirappalli](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tiruchirappalli), [Tamil Nadu](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tamil_Nadu), [India](https://grokipedia.com/page/India), specializing in the production of [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) rifles, machine guns, [grenade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Grenade) launchers, and related ammunition for the [Indian Armed Forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Armed_Forces).\[1\] Inaugurated on 3 July 1966 by [Prime Minister](https://grokipedia.com/page/Prime_minister) [Indira Gandhi](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indira_Gandhi), the factory began production in 1967 to enhance India's indigenous defense capabilities amid growing military needs.\[1\]\[2\] Following the 2021 corporatization of the [Ordnance Factory Board](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ordnance_Factory_Board), OFT operates as a unit of Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited (AWEIL), focusing on advanced weapon systems and export potential while maintaining self-reliance in arms production.\[3\] Notable products include the 7.62 mm Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), 5.56 mm [INSAS rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/INSAS_rifle) variants, 30 mm automatic [grenade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Grenade) launchers, and anti-material rifles, which have equipped Indian [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) and supported operational readiness.\[2\]\[4\] The facility has achieved milestones in indigenization, such as developing multi-caliber weapons and delivering specialized carbines to [paramilitary](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paramilitary) forces, underscoring its role in modernizing India's small arms inventory despite challenges from organizational restructuring that prompted employee protests.\[4\]\[5\]

Historical Development
----------------------

### Establishment and Early Operations (1960s-1980s)

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) was established in 1967 as part of India's post-independence expansion of defense manufacturing [infrastructure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infrastructure) to achieve self-reliance in arms production following the 1962 [Sino-Indian War](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sino-Indian_War). The facility, located in [Tiruchirappalli](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tiruchirappalli), [Tamil Nadu](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tamil_Nadu), was designed to augment the Ordnance Factories Board's capacity for [small arms and light weapons](https://grokipedia.com/page/Small_arms_and_light_weapons), addressing shortages in indigenous output amid geopolitical tensions with neighboring countries.\[6\] Initial [infrastructure](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infrastructure) development included [machine tool](https://grokipedia.com/page/Machine_tool) installations, assembly lines, and quality testing setups imported or adapted from licensed foreign technologies, with operations commencing that year under the Department of Defence Production. Early production at OFT centered on 7.62 mm rifles, which formed the backbone of [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) armament for the [Indian Army](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Army) during the period. These rifles, produced via licensed designs similar to the British [L1A1 self-loading rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/L1A1_Self-Loading_Rifle), enabled serial manufacturing to equip frontline units, with output scaled to meet annual defense indents. By the late [1960s](https://grokipedia.com/page/1960s), the factory had achieved initial production targets, incorporating precision machining for barrels and receivers to ensure reliability in tropical climates. Complementary items such as rifle spares and accessories were also manufactured, reducing dependency on imports for [maintenance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Maintenance). During the [1970s](https://grokipedia.com/page/1970s) and [1980s](https://grokipedia.com/page/1980s), OFT expanded operations to include 12.7 mm air defense guns and associated spares, supporting anti-aircraft capabilities for ground forces. This phase involved process refinements, such as [heat treatment](https://grokipedia.com/page/Heat_Treatment) for gun barrels and ballistic testing protocols, amid the 1971 Indo-Pakistani War and subsequent border skirmishes, which heightened demand for rapid replenishment. Workforce training programs were implemented to handle complex assembly, with the factory contributing to overcapacity buildup in [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) to buffer against supply disruptions. By the [1980s](https://grokipedia.com/page/1980s), annual production volumes for [rifles](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Rifles) exceeded thousands of units, though challenges like [technology transfer](https://grokipedia.com/page/Technology_transfer) delays from foreign licensors occasionally impacted timelines.\[6\]

### Expansion and Post-Cold War Adaptations (1990s-2010s)

In the 1990s, Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) underwent significant expansion to bolster India's domestic small arms production amid the post-Cold War shift toward greater self-reliance in defense manufacturing. Serial production of the indigenous 5.56 mm INSAS assault rifle commenced in 1994, enabling the factory to scale output for the Indian Army's modernization needs following the obsolescence of earlier 7.62 mm designs.\[1\] By 1997, mass production of both the INSAS rifle and its light machine gun variant was achieved, with initial units publicly showcased at the 1998 Republic Day parade, reflecting accelerated indigenization efforts to reduce foreign dependency.\[7\] The 1998 Pokhran-II nuclear tests triggered international sanctions, intensifying pressure on Indian ordnance facilities like OFT to enhance self-sufficiency and mitigate supply disruptions from traditional partners.\[8\] OFT responded by prioritizing high-volume INSAS production, contributing to the equipping of central forces and [paramilitary](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paramilitary) units, though reliability concerns emerged during operations like the 1999 [Kargil](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kargil) conflict, prompting iterative design adaptations without halting output.\[9\] Into the 2000s, OFT diversified its capabilities, establishing [production](https://grokipedia.com/page/Production) lines in 1999 for the 12.7 mm air defence gun and 0.32 calibre pistol to address varied tactical requirements across services.\[1\] The factory maintained peak capacities exceeding 30,000 rifles annually across Ordnance Factories Board units, with OFT as the primary [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) hub, supporting exports and internal demands despite global technology access constraints.\[10\] In the [2010s](https://grokipedia.com/page/2010s), adaptations included prototyping upgraded INSAS variants like the 1C [carbine](https://grokipedia.com/page/Carbine) for close-quarters use, alongside early work on the 7.62 mm Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) to offer alternatives to imported AK patterns, aligning with evolving [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) doctrines favoring multi-calibre flexibility.\[11\] These efforts underscored OFT's pivot from licensed replication to innovative, sanction-resilient [production](https://grokipedia.com/page/Production), though persistent quality critiques highlighted challenges in matching global standards.\[9\]

### Corporatization and Structural Reforms (2021-Present)

In July 2021, the Union Cabinet of [India](https://grokipedia.com/page/India) approved the corporatization of the [Ordnance Factory Board](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ordnance_Factory_Board) (OFB), dissolving the holding entity and reorganizing its 41 production units into seven independent 100% government-owned Defence [Public Sector Undertakings](https://grokipedia.com/page/Public_sector_undertakings) (DPSUs) effective October 1, 2021, to enhance operational autonomy, financial accountability, and market competitiveness while addressing longstanding issues of inefficiency and delays in the legacy OFB structure.\[12\] Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) was integrated into Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited (AWEIL), one of the new DPSUs headquartered in [Kanpur](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kanpur), [Uttar Pradesh](https://grokipedia.com/page/Uttar_Pradesh), which oversees manufacturing of [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army), ammunition, and related equipment from units including OFT.\[13\] This shift granted AWEIL, and by extension OFT, greater flexibility in procurement, [human resource management](https://grokipedia.com/page/Human_resource_management), and business operations compared to the centralized OFB model, with the stated aim of fostering [innovation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Innovation) and [self-reliance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-Reliance) in defence production.\[14\] The reforms faced initial resistance from OFB employees, including calls for indefinite strikes in July 2021 over concerns regarding [job security](https://grokipedia.com/page/Job_security) and [pension](https://grokipedia.com/page/Pension) benefits, though these actions largely subsided without significant disruption.\[15\] Post-corporatization, AWEIL and its units, including OFT, reported operational improvements aligned with broader DPSU outcomes, such as six of the seven entities achieving profitability and the group securing record export orders worth ₹3,500 [crore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crore) in [fiscal year](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fiscal_year) 2024-25, reflecting enhanced global competitiveness.\[16\] At OFT specifically, structural changes emphasized process upgradation and technical advancement in [weapon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Weapon) production, evidenced by initiatives in October 2025 soliciting innovative ideas from employees to optimize [manufacturing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Manufacturing) and encourage dialogue on R&D enhancements.\[17\] These reforms positioned OFT within AWEIL's framework for diversified revenue streams, including potential exports and [private sector](https://grokipedia.com/page/Private_sector) collaborations, though challenges persist in fully realizing autonomy amid government oversight and legacy workforce integration.\[18\] By 2025, AWEIL marked its fourth [foundation day](https://grokipedia.com/page/Foundation_Day) with events at OFT, underscoring ongoing adaptation to the corporatized model focused on sustained production capacity and technological upgrades.\[3\]

Products and Capabilities
-------------------------

### Small Arms Production

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) initiated [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) production in 1967 with 9 mm carbines to bolster India's domestic manufacturing capacity alongside Rifle Factory Ishapore and Small Arms Factory [Kanpur](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kanpur).\[19\] Over time, its portfolio expanded to include rifles chambered in various calibers, such as the 7.62 mm [Self-Loading Rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-loading_rifle) (SLR), 5.56 mm [INSAS Rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/INSAS_rifle), and .315 Sporting Rifle, supporting the [Indian armed forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Armed_Forces) and civilian markets.\[20\] These efforts contributed to self-reliance in [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) weaponry, with production emphasizing licensed designs and indigenous adaptations.\[21\] A key development was the [Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assault_rifle), a 7.62x39 mm design conceived in 2015 as an [AK-47](https://grokipedia.com/page/AK-47) equivalent for enhanced reliability in adverse conditions. Production commenced at OFT in 2017, with the first batch of 500 units delivered to the [Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Central_Reserve_Police_Force) on March 13, 2020.\[22\] The TAR features a fixed buttstock variant and has seen adoption by [paramilitary](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paramilitary) units, including a 2024 order for 125 additional units by the [Border Security Force (BSF)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Border_Security_Force) complete with bayonets.\[23\] Derivatives like the compact Baby TAR, leveraging TAR manufacturing experience, further diversified OFT's offerings for close-quarters applications.\[24\] OFT also manufactures the Multi-Caliber Individual Weapon System (MCIWS), developed in collaboration with the DRDO's [Armament Research and Development Establishment](https://grokipedia.com/page/Armament_Research_and_Development_Establishment), enabling caliber switches between 5.56 mm, 7.62 mm, and .350 mm for versatile [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) use.\[25\] Following corporatization into [Advanced Weapons and Equipment India](https://grokipedia.com/page/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India) Limited in 2021, production continues to prioritize quality and scalability, though specific output volumes remain classified. These [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) underscore OFT's role in transitioning from legacy systems like the SLR to modern, [indigenous](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indigenous) platforms amid India's [defense](https://grokipedia.com/page/Defense) [indigenization](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indigenization) drive.\[1\]

### Heavy Weapon Systems and Accessories

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) produces the [AGS-30](https://grokipedia.com/page/AGS-30), a 30 mm [automatic grenade launcher](https://grokipedia.com/page/Automatic_grenade_launcher) developed under license from [Russian](https://grokipedia.com/page/Russian) designs, offering enhanced mobility, [range](https://grokipedia.com/page/Range) up to 2,100 [meters](https://grokipedia.com/page/The_Meters), a [rate of fire](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rate_of_fire) of 400 grenades per minute, and improved accuracy compared to predecessors like the AGS-17.\[26\] This system supports infantry suppression and area denial roles within the [Indian armed forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Armed_Forces).\[27\] In collaboration with foreign technology partners, OFT manufactures the Stabilized Remote Controlled [Gun](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gun) (SRCG), equipped with a 12.7 mm M2 NATO-standard [heavy machine gun](https://grokipedia.com/page/Heavy_machine_gun) for naval and coastal applications.\[28\] On [July 17](https://grokipedia.com/page/July_17), 2021, OFT delivered 15 SRCG units to the [Indian Navy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Navy) and 10 to the [Indian Coast Guard](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Coast_Guard), enabling remote operation from protected positions on ships and surveillance craft to engage surface threats effectively.\[29\] The system incorporates electro-optic fire control for stabilized firing, reducing crew exposure during operations.\[30\] OFT also supports production of [rocket-propelled grenade](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rocket-propelled_grenade) systems, including the [RPG-7](https://grokipedia.com/page/RPG-7) launcher, which fires 40 mm PG-7 series warheads capable of penetrating armored vehicles and fortifications at ranges exceeding 200 meters for point targets.\[31\] Accessories such as stabilization mounts, optical sights, and ammunition feeds are integrated into these platforms to enhance operational reliability in diverse terrains.\[27\] These contributions bolster India's [self-reliance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-Reliance) in crew-served heavy weapons for land and [maritime](https://grokipedia.com/page/Maritime) defense.

### Licensed and Indigenous Designs

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) manufactures several [weapon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Weapon) systems under foreign licenses, primarily from [Russian](https://grokipedia.com/page/Russian) designs, to meet [Indian armed forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Armed_Forces)' requirements. The [AGS-30](https://grokipedia.com/page/AGS-30) 30 mm [automatic grenade launcher](https://grokipedia.com/page/Automatic_grenade_launcher) is produced under license from Russia's [KBP Instrument Design Bureau](https://grokipedia.com/page/KBP_Instrument_Design_Bureau), utilizing 30x29 mm grenades and serving as a man-portable [fire support](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fire_support) [weapon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Weapon).\[26\] OFT has also engaged in licensed production of the [OSV-96](https://grokipedia.com/page/OSV-96) 12.7x108 mm anti-[materiel](https://grokipedia.com/page/Materiel) [sniper rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Sniper_rifle), a [Russian](https://grokipedia.com/page/Russian) system adapted for precision long-range engagements against materiel targets. In parallel, OFT has developed indigenous designs to enhance [self-reliance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-Reliance) in small arms production. The Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), a 7.62x39 mm [assault rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assault_rifle), was designed and developed by OFT in 2011 to match [AK-47](https://grokipedia.com/page/AK-47) specifications, featuring improvements for reliability and local [manufacturing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Manufacturing).\[32\] Variants include the compact "Baby TAR" or TriCa, introduced for [special forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Special_forces) with telescoping or folding stocks, with nearly 20,000 units produced by 2021.\[33\] The [Vidhwansak](https://grokipedia.com/page/Vidhwansak) multi-caliber [anti-materiel rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Anti-materiel_rifle), capable of firing 12.7 mm, [.50 BMG](https://grokipedia.com/page/.50_BMG), and 20 mm rounds, was unveiled by OFT on August 13, 2020, as an in-house development for counter-materiel roles.\[34\] OFT's indigenous efforts extend to advanced systems like the Stabilized Remote Controlled Gun (SRCG), a remotely operated weapon station, with orders for 463 units secured for the [Indian Navy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Navy) in 2024, emphasizing modular integration on naval platforms.\[35\] These designs reflect OFT's focus on achieving high [indigenization](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indigenization) levels, reported at 94% across its portfolio under [Advanced Weapons and Equipment India](https://grokipedia.com/page/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India) Limited.\[36\]

Technological and Manufacturing Processes
-----------------------------------------

### Research and Development Initiatives

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) has pursued [research and development](https://grokipedia.com/page/Research_and_development) initiatives centered on enhancing [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) capabilities, emphasizing indigenous designs for [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) and [special forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Special_forces) requirements. These efforts, often conducted in-house with technical support from the [Armament Research and Development Establishment](https://grokipedia.com/page/Armament_Research_and_Development_Establishment) (ARDE) of DRDO, aim to address gaps in firepower, ergonomics, and modularity while reducing reliance on foreign imports.\[37\] A flagship project is the 7.62 mm [Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assault_rifle), developed by OFT starting in 2015 to provide a robust alternative to licensed designs like the [AK-47](https://grokipedia.com/page/AK-47), with production commencing in 2017 and initial deliveries of 200 units to [paramilitary](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paramilitary) forces in [Chandigarh](https://grokipedia.com/page/Chandigarh) by March 2020.\[38\]\[39\] The TAR features [selective fire](https://grokipedia.com/page/Selective_fire) modes for single and burst shooting, weighing approximately 3.4 kg unloaded, and has been adopted by units such as the [CRPF](https://grokipedia.com/page/CRPF) and BSF for [close-quarters combat](https://grokipedia.com/page/Close-quarters_combat) effectiveness.\[40\] In parallel, OFT indigenized the TriCa 7.62x39 mm [carbine](https://grokipedia.com/page/Carbine) through internal R&D, launching it in July 2021 as a compact [weapon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Weapon) (3.5 kg loaded, submachine gun dimensions) suited for urban operations and [law enforcement](https://grokipedia.com/page/Law_enforcement).\[41\] Deliveries include 92 units to [Kerala Police](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kerala_Police) in May 2025 and orders for NSG, demonstrating sustained production scaling.\[5\] OFT advanced anti-materiel capabilities with the launch of an indigenous 12.7 mm Anti-Material Rifle (AMR), known as Vidhwansak, in August 2020, capable of engaging armored targets and personnel at extended ranges up to 1,500 meters.\[34\] This multi-caliber system, produced using existing infrastructure, supports a five-year workload and aligns with Army trials for sniper roles.\[42\] Additional R&D encompasses accessories like the 40 mm under-barrel [grenade launcher](https://grokipedia.com/page/Grenade_launcher) (UBGL) and trials for TAR [carbine](https://grokipedia.com/page/Carbine) variants, initiated around 2019 to bolster squad-level firepower.\[43\] OFT also developed the Stabilised [Remote Control](https://grokipedia.com/page/Remote_control) [Gun](https://grokipedia.com/page/Gun) (SRCG) for naval applications, with manufacturing underway by February 2024 to equip patrol vessels.\[35\] Under Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited (AWEIL), OFT's parent entity post-2021 corporatization, R&D receives heightened investment for modern systems, including employee-driven innovations solicited in October 2025 to drive incremental improvements.\[44\]\[17\] These initiatives contribute to India's [self-reliance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-Reliance) in defense, though production scales remain modest compared to [private sector](https://grokipedia.com/page/Private_sector) entrants.

### Quality Control and Production Technologies

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) implements a [Quality Management System](https://grokipedia.com/page/Quality_management_system) certified to ISO 9001:2015, which establishes documented procedures for process control, [risk assessment](https://grokipedia.com/page/Risk_assessment), and corrective actions across manufacturing operations.\[1\] This system integrates with broader certifications including ISO 14001:2015 for environmental management and [ISO 45001](https://grokipedia.com/page/ISO_45001):2018 for occupational health and safety, fostering a unified approach to operational reliability.\[45\] Compliance is verified through internal audits and third-party surveillance, with non-conformities addressed via root-cause analysis to minimize defects in [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) production. The factory's in-house laboratories hold National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) accreditation in mechanical and chemical disciplines, supporting precise material testing, such as tensile strength evaluations and [chemical composition](https://grokipedia.com/page/Chemical_composition) analysis for alloys used in [rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rifle) components.\[46\] Products undergo stage-wise quality checks, including dimensional inspections with coordinate measuring machines, non-destructive testing for internal flaws, and ballistic trials to validate performance against specifications outlined in [Quality Assurance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Quality_assurance) Plans.\[47\] These measures ensure adherence to [defense](https://grokipedia.com/page/Defense) standards, with rejection rates tracked to refine processes. Production technologies at OFT feature computer [numerical control](https://grokipedia.com/page/Numerical_control) (CNC) machines for high-precision [machining](https://grokipedia.com/page/Machining) of components like barrels, bolts, and receivers, enabling tolerances as fine as 0.01 mm in small arms fabrication.\[1\] Automated [forging](https://grokipedia.com/page/Forging), [heat treatment](https://grokipedia.com/page/Heat_Treatment) furnaces, and [electroplating](https://grokipedia.com/page/Electroplating) lines support scalable output, while integration of CAD/[CAM](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cam) software optimizes tool paths and reduces material waste.\[48\] These capabilities extend to licensed productions, such as grenade launchers, where transfer of technology from foreign principals is adapted via [reverse engineering](https://grokipedia.com/page/Reverse_engineering) and iterative prototyping to meet indigenous requirements.\[49\]

### Adoption of Foreign and Domestic Innovations

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) has incorporated foreign technologies primarily through [licensed production](https://grokipedia.com/page/Licensed_production) and [technology transfer](https://grokipedia.com/page/Technology_transfer) agreements, enabling the manufacture of advanced systems tailored for Indian defense needs. In 2021, OFT delivered 15 units of the 12.7 mm M2 [NATO](https://grokipedia.com/page/NATO) Stabilized Remote Control Guns following a [technology transfer](https://grokipedia.com/page/Technology_transfer) from [Elbit Systems](https://grokipedia.com/page/Elbit_Systems) of [Israel](https://grokipedia.com/page/Israel), designed for remote operation in marine applications to enhance naval firepower without exposing personnel.\[29\]\[50\] These guns, produced under direct foreign collaboration, represent a shift from earlier [self-reliance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-Reliance) efforts, addressing gaps in stabilized remote weaponry through imported expertise. Broader policy changes in 2008 permitted [ordnance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ordnance) factories, including OFT, to pursue advanced [technology](https://grokipedia.com/page/Technology) tie-ups with international firms, facilitating such integrations to modernize [production](https://grokipedia.com/page/Production) capabilities.\[51\] Domestically, OFT has focused on indigenous development to reduce reliance on imports, collaborating with entities like the [Armament Research and Development Establishment](https://grokipedia.com/page/Armament_Research_and_Development_Establishment) (ARDE) for design and prototyping. The 7.62×39 mm Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), an indigenous automatic [weapon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Weapon) comparable to the [AK-47](https://grokipedia.com/page/AK-47) in specifications, was developed by OFT starting in 2015, with production lines established by 2017; the first batch of 500 units was supplied to the [Central Reserve Police Force](https://grokipedia.com/page/Central_Reserve_Police_Force) (CRPF) in March 2020.\[38\]\[39\] This [rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Rifle), chambered for effective [close-quarters combat](https://grokipedia.com/page/Close-quarters_combat), incorporates local metallurgical and ergonomic adaptations, marking a key innovation in paramilitary-grade small arms. Complementing this, OFT launched the TriCa [carbine](https://grokipedia.com/page/Carbine) in July 2021, a compact, low-signature [weapon](https://grokipedia.com/page/Weapon) with superior range over standard submachine guns, including variants with folding stocks; by May 2025, deliveries included 92 units to [Kerala Police](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kerala_Police), demonstrating iterative domestic refinements in suppressed firearms.\[52\]\[41\] These adoptions reflect a pragmatic balance: foreign transfers for specialized, high-tech components where indigenous capabilities lag, paired with domestic R&D to build self-sustaining production ecosystems, as evidenced by OFT's employee-driven [innovation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Innovation) sessions in October 2025 aimed at [process](https://grokipedia.com/page/Process) upgrades in weapon manufacturing.\[17\] Such efforts align with national goals of technological sovereignty while leveraging global best practices for reliability and performance.

Operational Performance and Impact
----------------------------------

### Key Achievements and Milestones

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) was established in 1966 to bolster India's [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) manufacturing capacity, with initial [production](https://grokipedia.com/page/Production) of 9 mm carbines commencing in 1967 and [expansion](https://grokipedia.com/page/Expansion) to 7.62 mm rifles by the mid-1970s.\[9\]\[53\] The facility marked its [golden jubilee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Golden_jubilee) in 2016, highlighting five decades of contributions to national defense through consistent output of infantry weapons.\[54\] OFT achieved prominence as the leading producer of the INSAS 5.56 mm [assault rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assault_rifle), supplying the highest volumes to the [Indian armed forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Armed_Forces) and paramilitary units.\[9\] In 2011, it developed the indigenous Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), a 7.62x39 mm design based on AK patterns, enhancing options for close-quarter combat needs.\[32\] A key technological milestone came in July 2021 with the handover of the first 25 units of 12.7 mm M2 NATO standard Stabilized Remote Control Gun systems—15 to the [Indian Navy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Navy) and 10 to the Coast Guard—assembled via technology transfer from Elbit Systems of [Israel](https://grokipedia.com/page/Israel), featuring advanced remote targeting with thermal imaging and [laser](https://grokipedia.com/page/Laser) rangefinders.\[55\] More recently, in May 2025, OFT delivered the initial batch of 7.62x39 mm TriCa carbines to the [Kerala Police](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kerala_Police), demonstrating ongoing adaptation to specialized law enforcement requirements.\[5\] The factory maintains ISO 9001:2015, ISO 14001:2015, ISO 45001:2018 (formerly [OHSAS 18001](https://grokipedia.com/page/OHSAS_18001)), and ISO 50001:2011 certifications, underscoring its [quality management](https://grokipedia.com/page/Quality_management) and [energy efficiency](https://grokipedia.com/page/Energy_efficiency) standards.\[48\]

### Efficiency Metrics and Economic Contributions

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) demonstrated production efficiency through its output of [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) during the 2020–21 [fiscal year](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fiscal_year), manufacturing and dispatching weapons valued at ₹160 [crore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crore), including over 11,000 Trichy Assault Rifles to meet [Indian Army](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Army) requirements.\[56\] This output reflects the factory's capacity as India's largest [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) producer, with diversified lines encompassing rifles, machine guns, and grenade launchers, enabling scalable fulfillment of defense orders amid operational constraints like the [COVID-19](https://grokipedia.com/page/COVID-19) disruptions prevalent at the time. Post-corporatization in 2021, OFT's integration into Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited (AWEIL) aligned with broader reforms that enhanced productivity across erstwhile [Ordnance Factory Board](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ordnance_Factory_Board) units, evidenced by the seven new defense public sector undertakings achieving record exports of ₹3,500 [crore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crore) and consistent profitability in 2024–25.\[16\] Economically, OFT contributes to Tiruchirappalli's industrial base, a key driver in [Tamil](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tamil) Nadu's defense manufacturing ecosystem, by generating direct employment for skilled workers in [precision engineering](https://grokipedia.com/page/Precision_engineering) and supporting ancillary supply chains for components and [logistics](https://grokipedia.com/page/Logistics). As part of the corporatized structure, OFT bolsters national defense self-reliance under initiatives like "[Atmanirbhar Bharat](https://grokipedia.com/page/Atmanirbhar_Bharat)," reducing import dependence on small arms and fostering technology transfer in indigenous designs such as the Trichy Assault Rifle. The factory's operations indirectly stimulate regional economic activity through procurement of raw materials and maintenance services, though specific revenue attribution remains aggregated within AWEIL's performance metrics, which mirror the improved financial health of reformed [ordnance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ordnance) entities with profits reported across the group.\[57\] These contributions underscore OFT's role in sustaining employment stability—drawing from the legacy of over 164,000 personnel across the original [Ordnance Factory Board](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ordnance_Factory_Board)—and enhancing export potential for defense products.\[58\]

### Criticisms, Challenges, and Controversies

The INSAS [assault rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assault_rifle), a primary product manufactured at Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT), encountered persistent reliability issues that drew criticism from [Indian armed forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Armed_Forces) users, including frequent jamming, magazine cracks under stress, and malfunctions in [extreme weather](https://grokipedia.com/page/Extreme_weather) conditions such as high altitudes and cold environments during operations like the Kargil conflict in 1999.\[59\]\[7\] These defects stemmed from design flaws in polymer components and gas systems, leading to phased reductions in procurement by the [Army](https://grokipedia.com/page/Army), which halted bulk orders post-2015 in favor of alternatives like the AK-203.\[60\]\[61\] OFT has grappled with procurement and production delays, exemplified by a 2015 Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) report documenting delays in order placement for 69 percent of instances at the facility, exacerbating supply chain inefficiencies and contributing to broader Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) shortfalls in meeting defense timelines.\[62\] Overall production volumes at OFT declined notably by the mid-2010s, with output for key small arms like the 7.62 mm Trichy Assault Rifle failing to scale despite introductions to replace INSAS variants, amid reports of underutilized capacity and stagnant demand from military clients.\[9\]\[63\] The 2021 corporatization of OFB into entities like Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited (AWEIL), which absorbed OFT's small arms operations, sparked internal controversies, with Tiruchirappalli employees protesting the restructuring on October 1, 2021, by boycotting lunch and observing a "Black Day" over fears of job insecurity, reduced pensions, and privatization risks despite government assurances of no layoffs.\[64\] Critics, including defense unions, argued the reform failed to address core inefficiencies like high costs and substandard quality—issues the Ministry of Defence had publicly highlighted in 2019 as plaguing OFB products, including those from OFT—while subsequent reports in 2022 labeled the transition an "utter failure" for not improving productivity or competitiveness.\[65\]\[66\] These challenges reflect systemic issues in government-run defense manufacturing, such as monopolistic structures limiting innovation and accountability, though OFT has continued fulfilling niche orders like Stabilised [Remote Control](https://grokipedia.com/page/Remote_control) Guns for the [Navy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Navy) in 2024, indicating selective operational resilience amid ongoing reforms.\[35\]\[67\]

Customers and Strategic Role
----------------------------

### Domestic Military and Paramilitary Users

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli's primary domestic customers include the [Indian Army](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Army), Navy, Air Force, and Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) such as the [Central Reserve Police Force](https://grokipedia.com/page/Central_Reserve_Police_Force) (CRPF), [Border Security Force](https://grokipedia.com/page/Border_Security_Force) (BSF), and [Central Industrial Security Force](https://grokipedia.com/page/Central_Industrial_Security_Force) (CISF). The factory supplies small arms, machine guns, grenade launchers, and naval gun systems tailored to these entities' operational requirements.\[1\] The 7.62 mm [Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assault_rifle), a key product, has been adopted mainly by [paramilitary](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paramilitary) forces for counter-insurgency and border security roles. In March 2020, the first batch of 500 TAR rifles was delivered to the [CRPF](https://grokipedia.com/page/CRPF). By March 2021, over 11,500 TAR units had been supplied to various CAPF units, including the [CRPF](https://grokipedia.com/page/CRPF). In January 2024, the BSF procured an additional 125 TAR rifles equipped with bayonets and accessories.\[56\]\[23\] For maritime applications, OFT provides stabilized remote-controlled gun systems to the [Indian Navy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Navy) and [Indian Coast Guard](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Coast_Guard). In July 2021, the factory handed over 15 units of the 12.7 mm M2 [NATO](https://grokipedia.com/page/NATO) Stabilized Remote Control Gun to the [Navy](https://grokipedia.com/page/Navy) and 10 units to the Coast Guard for shipboard defense. These systems enhance remote weapon station capabilities on patrol vessels and warships.\[68\] Machine guns and grenade launchers from OFT equip armored vehicles and infantry units across the armed forces, including 7.62 mm coaxial and anti-aircraft guns integrated into main battle tanks like the [Arjun](https://grokipedia.com/page/Arjun), [T-72](https://grokipedia.com/page/T-72) Ajeya, and T-90 Bhishma, as well as infantry combat vehicles such as the BMP-2 Sarath. Paramilitary forces also receive multi-grenade launchers compatible with TAR rifles for area suppression in internal security operations.\[69\]

### Export Potential and International Engagements

[Advanced Weapons and Equipment India](https://grokipedia.com/page/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India) Limited (AWEIL), which operates Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT), secured export orders valued at approximately ₹700 crore as of recent reports, encompassing [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) and medium-calibre weapons produced at its facilities, including those specialized in rifles, machine guns, and grenade launchers.\[70\] These exports represent about 5 percent of AWEIL's revenues in the 2023-24 fiscal year, reflecting a 5 percent year-over-year increase and underscoring growing international demand for cost-effective, indigenously developed [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) weapons.\[71\] OFT's contributions to this portfolio include products like the 5.56 mm [INSAS rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/INSAS_rifle) variants and 7.62 mm Trichy Assault Rifle, which align with the requirements of [paramilitary](https://grokipedia.com/page/Paramilitary) and security forces in developing nations seeking reliable, battle-tested [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army).\[72\] The export potential of OFT's offerings is bolstered by AWEIL's 94 percent indigenization rate—one of the highest among Defence [Public Sector Undertakings](https://grokipedia.com/page/Public_sector_undertakings)—enabling competitive pricing against global competitors while maintaining [interoperability](https://grokipedia.com/page/Interoperability) with NATO-standard [ammunition](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ammunition) and accessories.\[72\] This positions OFT favorably for markets in [South Asia](https://grokipedia.com/page/South_Asia), [Southeast Asia](https://grokipedia.com/page/Southeast_Asia), and [Africa](https://grokipedia.com/page/Africa), where buyers prioritize affordability and proven durability in adverse conditions over cutting-edge features. Ongoing [corporatization](https://grokipedia.com/page/Corporatization) reforms have streamlined marketing through dedicated export divisions, facilitating participation in international tenders and defence expos, with projections for further growth tied to India's broader defence export targets exceeding ₹35,000 [crore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crore) annually across all [public sector](https://grokipedia.com/page/Public_sector) units.\[16\] On the international front, OFT has pursued engagements primarily through licensed [manufacturing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Manufacturing) and [technology](https://grokipedia.com/page/Technology) transfers to upgrade its production lines. In [2021](https://grokipedia.com/page/2021), the factory produced an initial batch of 25 heavy machine guns incorporating [Israeli](https://grokipedia.com/page/Israeli) design and [technology](https://grokipedia.com/page/Technology), demonstrating successful adaptation of foreign [precision engineering](https://grokipedia.com/page/Precision_engineering) for enhanced reliability in anti-aircraft and vehicle-mounted roles.\[73\] Such collaborations extend to other licensed products, including grenade launchers and autocannons derived from foreign originals, which OFT modifies for local needs while retaining core performance metrics. These partnerships not only diversify OFT's technological base but also signal to potential exporters its capacity for joint ventures, potentially leading to co-production deals that mitigate geopolitical risks in arms trade.\[1\]

### Alignment with National Defense Self-Reliance Goals

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) supports India's national defense self-reliance objectives, embodied in initiatives like [Atmanirbhar Bharat](https://grokipedia.com/page/Atmanirbhar_Bharat), by producing indigenous small arms and related systems that equip the armed forces domestically. Key products include the 7.62 mm Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), developed and manufactured at OFT to meet [Indian Army](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Army) requirements for reliable, locally sourced [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) weapons, thereby reducing dependence on imported [assault rifles](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assault_rifle). Similarly, OFT's production of the 5.56 mm [INSAS rifle](https://grokipedia.com/page/INSAS_rifle), though facing reliability critiques, has historically fulfilled bulk procurement needs, contributing to self-sufficiency in basic [infantry](https://grokipedia.com/page/Infantry) armament since the 1990s. These efforts align with the government's push to indigenize 70-80% of defense inventory by prioritizing public sector units like OFT for core munitions.\[74\] OFT's innovations, such as the indigenously designed Stabilized Remote-Controlled Gun (SRCG) launched in August 2020, exemplify technological [self-reliance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-Reliance) by integrating electro-optical sensors and fire control systems for unmanned vehicle mounting, without foreign components. This system enhances armored platform capabilities for the [Indian Army](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indian_Army), supporting operational autonomy in border defense scenarios. Through such developments, OFT has aided in curbing import reliance for specialized armaments, as evidenced by the broader ordnance sector's role in achieving near-100% self-sufficiency in certain [ammunition](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ammunition) categories by 2024. The factory's output, including grenade launchers and anti-aircraft guns, directly feeds into the Defense Production Policy's emphasis on domestic [manufacturing](https://grokipedia.com/page/Manufacturing) to minimize strategic vulnerabilities from [supply chain](https://grokipedia.com/page/Supply_chain) disruptions.\[75\]\[76\] Post-2021 corporatization of the [Ordnance Factory Board](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ordnance_Factory_Board) into entities like [Advanced Weapons and Equipment India](https://grokipedia.com/page/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India) Limited, which oversees OFT, has streamlined operations to better align with [self-reliance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-Reliance) goals by introducing professional management and performance incentives. This reform, part of Atmanirbhar Bharat's defense pillar, aims to boost production efficiency and export potential, with corporatized units securing record orders exceeding ₹3,500 crore in 2024-25, including [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) from facilities like OFT. Despite persistent challenges in scaling user acceptance for some indigenous designs, OFT's focus on iterative improvements and integration with DRDO-developed technologies reinforces causal pathways to reduced import bills, estimated at over $5 billion annually pre-reforms, fostering economic sovereignty in defense procurement.\[77\]\[16\]

Future Outlook and Reforms
--------------------------

### Post-Corporatization Developments

Following the corporatization of the Ordnance Factory Board into seven Defence Public Sector Undertakings effective October 1, 2021, Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) was integrated as a key production unit under Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited (AWEIL), specializing in small arms manufacturing.\[1\] This restructuring granted AWEIL, including OFT, enhanced autonomy in operations, procurement, and market expansion compared to the prior centralized board structure.\[78\] Post-integration, OFT focused on upgrading product lines and [indigenization](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indigenization), achieving 94% indigenous content across AWEIL's portfolio by 2024 through targeted facility modernizations and [supply chain](https://grokipedia.com/page/Supply_chain) localization efforts.\[72\] A notable product advancement was the 2021 introduction of the Prahaar, an updated 0.32-inch [revolver](https://grokipedia.com/page/Revolver) variant designed for improved reliability and user handling in security applications.\[1\] A key milestone occurred on May 9, 2025, when OFT delivered the initial batch of 92 [TriCa (Trichy Carbine)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Carbine) 7.62x39mm compact [carbines](https://grokipedia.com/page/Carbine)—optimized for [close-quarters battle](https://grokipedia.com/page/Close_combat), infantry combat vehicles, and [helicopter](https://grokipedia.com/page/Helicopter) crews—to the [Kerala Police](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kerala_Police), fulfilling a 2022 order.\[79\] Additional TriCa orders include supplies to the Assam Forest Department, [Central Bureau of Narcotics](https://grokipedia.com/page/Central_Bureau_of_Narcotics), and 100 units for the [National Security Guard](https://grokipedia.com/page/National_Security_Guard), demonstrating expanded domestic demand for OFT's indigenous designs.\[41\] To drive internal [innovation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Innovation), OFT initiated employee-suggested improvements programs in October 2025, aiming to enhance [production](https://grokipedia.com/page/Production) [efficiency](https://grokipedia.com/page/Efficiency) and product [development](https://grokipedia.com/page/Development).\[17\] The unit also marked AWEIL's foundation day on October 3, 2025, underscoring sustained operational momentum under the new corporate framework.\[18\] AWEIL's overall sales reached ₹1,900 [crore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crore) in fiscal year 2022-23, up from ₹1,076 [crore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crore) in the partial post-corporatization year, reflecting broader gains in [order fulfillment](https://grokipedia.com/page/Order_fulfillment) and market responsiveness.\[70\]

### Ongoing Projects and Expansion Plans

Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli continues production of the 7.62×39 mm [Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Assault_rifle), which remains in high demand by [Central Armed Police Forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Central_Armed_Police_Forces) as of 2024.\[72\] In May 2025, the factory delivered 92 [Trichy Carbine (TriCa)](https://grokipedia.com/page/Carbine) rifles to the [Kerala Police](https://grokipedia.com/page/Kerala_Police), fulfilling a 2022 order for these compact 7.62×39 mm weapons designed for vehicle crews, paratroopers, and [special forces](https://grokipedia.com/page/Special_forces).\[41\]\[79\] AWEIL, overseeing OFT, has prioritized modern [weapon system](https://grokipedia.com/page/Weapon_System) development with increased R&D investment as of early 2025, targeting 100% indigenisation from 94%.\[44\]\[72\] In [October](https://grokipedia.com/page/October) 2025, OFT held employee innovation sessions to drive technical advancements and process upgrades in small arms manufacturing.\[17\] Expansion efforts include capacity enhancements via new plants and machinery, aligning with DPSU-wide modernization to boost output for defense requirements.\[80\] A February 2024 contract with the [Ministry of Defence](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ministry_of_defence) supports indigenous production of 12.7 mm weapons, extending OFT's role in heavier armaments.\[72\]

### Implications of Market-Oriented Reforms

The corporatization of the [Ordnance Factory Board](https://grokipedia.com/page/Ordnance_Factory_Board) into seven defence [public sector undertakings](https://grokipedia.com/page/Public_sector_undertakings) in July 2021, placing Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli under [Advanced Weapons and Equipment India](https://grokipedia.com/page/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India) Limited (AWEIL), introduced market-oriented dynamics by emphasizing profit accountability, operational autonomy, and competition with private entities. This reform addressed chronic inefficiencies, such as delivery delays and quality shortfalls in [small arms](https://grokipedia.com/page/List_of_equipment_of_the_Eritrean_Army) production, by enabling faster [decision-making](https://grokipedia.com/page/Decision-making) and [resource allocation](https://grokipedia.com/page/Resource_allocation) akin to corporate models. Aggregate performance across the corporatized units shifted from a ₹2,844 [crore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crore) loss in 2019-20 to a ₹1,625 [crore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crore) profit in FY 2024-25, with six of seven entities achieving profitability through streamlined processes and diversified revenue streams.\[81\]\[82\] For OFT, these reforms imply heightened incentives for innovation in products like assault rifles and grenade launchers, fostering partnerships for technology upgrades and achieving 94% [indigenization](https://grokipedia.com/page/Indigenization) rates within AWEIL—among the highest for DPSUs—while targeting 100%. Exports from the former ordnance units reached a record ₹3,500 [crore](https://grokipedia.com/page/Crore) in 2024-25, signaling potential for OFT to capture international markets amid India's push for defence [self-reliance](https://grokipedia.com/page/Self-Reliance), though small arms demand from armed forces had been subdued pre-reform due to quality concerns.\[72\]\[16\]\[83\] Challenges persist, including workforce reductions from 144,000 to 58,903 across units and ongoing employee grievances over perceived harassment and job insecurity, with unions at OFT protesting the shift as a veiled path to [privatization](https://grokipedia.com/page/Privatization). Market pressures could erode OFT's [monopoly](https://grokipedia.com/page/Monopoly) on domestic orders if private competitors like [Tata](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tata) or [Larsen & Toubro](https://grokipedia.com/page/Larsen_&_Toubro) deliver superior timelines, necessitating sustained efficiency gains to avoid revenue erosion.\[84\]\[85\]\[86\]

![Image 1: The Border Security Force (BSF) is gearing up to equip its personnel with the Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR)](https://img.republicworld.com/rimages/GDm2Rp2asAAuysl-170530904042916_9.webp?w=1280&h=720&q=75&format=webp)

The Border Security Force to equip its personnel with the Trichy Assault Rifle. | Image: BSF India

**New Delhi:** The Border Security Force (BSF) is gearing up to equip its personnel with the Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), an indigenously developed firearm, according to an official statement. The procurement is set at a limited quantity, with the BSF acquiring 125 rifles along with bayonets and other accessory items.

TAR: Firepower Tailored for Specialised Needs of Paramilitary
-------------------------------------------------------------

The primary objective behind this move is to set an example for other wings of the Armed Forces and Paramilitary, encouraging them to follow suit and procure more indigenous arms. The initiative aims to strengthen India's self-sufficiency in defence capabilities.

![Image 2](https://www.republicworld.com/_app/immutable/assets/16-9-placeholder.ylpwvwO6.jpg)

“Ordnance Factory, Trichirappallin developed and manufactured TAR  Down folding butt version to meet the customer requirement as some of the CAPF units, State Police and RPF required the Down folding butt version for quick and easy movement of personnel in guard and patrolling duty”, said Officials in a prior statement.

Trichy Assault Rifle: Counter-Terror Operations with Cutting-Edge Firepower
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 3](https://www.republicworld.com/_app/immutable/assets/16-9-placeholder.ylpwvwO6.jpg)

*   The TAR, chambered in 7.62x39mm, has a lightweight modular design, making it well-suited for counter-insurgency and counter-terror operations. 
*   Its gas-operated mechanism, machined mono-block receiver body, and fibre-reinforced polymer magazine with steel inserts contribute to its effectiveness in the field. 
*   The rifle operates in both single-shot and burst modes, with the latter capable of destroying targets at a range of up to 500m. The TAR's overall destructive range extends to 1350m.
*   A customised version featuring a single-round firing mode is designed specifically for police forces engaged in patrolling duties within urban areas. The TAR-Down folding butt has an overall length of 900mm in the butt-open condition and 650mm in the butt-folding condition.
*   The rifle's versatility is further increased with the option to fit a 40x46mm UBGL GP-25, GP-30, and M6, catering to various operational requirements. Additionally, the inclusion of Tritium-filled sources for night firing and a Picatinny rail for mounting optical sights underlines the rifle’s adaptability to diverse scenarios.

Paramilitary and Police Forces with Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) in Active Service
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

![Image 4](https://www.republicworld.com/_app/immutable/assets/16-9-placeholder.ylpwvwO6.jpg)

In 2020, the Ordnance Factory of Tiruchirappalli (OFT) delivered the initial batch of 500 Trichy Assault Rifles (TAR) to the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), fulfilling a total order of 6,167 assault rifles.

The procurement followed rigorous field trials, including evaluation sessions at the CRPF Academy in Kadarpur, Haryana, in November 2017. Testing focused on the TAR's functionality, accuracy, and reliability, with 15,000 rounds fired without a single stoppage, affirming the weapon's dependability.

OFT has further supplied over 10,000 rifles to Chhattisgarh police and various central armed reserve police forces, including the ITBP, BSF, and CISF. Shirish Khare, OFT's General Manager had proudly acclaimed the Trichy Assault Rifle as their most significant success in the past 12-13 years of weapons development.

With a focus on promoting indigenous weaponry, the adoption of the TAR by the BSF signifies an important step in fortifying the nation's Paramilitary  security apparatus. This move aligns with broader initiatives to reduce dependence on foreign arms, fostering self-sufficiency in defence production.

Armament R&D Establishment Working On New Assault Rifle
=======================================================

Armament R&D Establishment Working On New Assault Rifle

Friday, February 16, 2018 by [Indian Defence News](https://www.blogger.com/profile/10039798451461108617)


===================================================================================================================================================================

![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEh9ew7eKASzkwQScLKFJhszoeadKBfRWBa3wB3pL4EoCVA2SYyVZxvFo_iXkB_UXxHl9wvTQ_1tfoNf8q4LBe2fLzsEjfm2HhwZj5flZ2zUG9ghYaZZiEwblz8e4A2Xpfq4-cbbK34TXZ2b/s1600/OFB_Trichy_Assault_Rifle.jpg)

**_Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) Trichy Assault Rifle_**

  

Even as the Defence Acquisition Council cleared the global procurement of 72,400 assault rifles and 93,895 carbines for the Army on a fast-track basis for ₹3,547 crore last month, trials of an assault rifle being developed by the Ordnance Factory Board (OFB) are to simultaneously continue unabated.

  

A new 5.56 assault rifle was developed by the Armament Research and Development Establishment (ARDE), Pune, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and the OFB.

  

“The OFB is in the process of development of the weapon and the same is planned to be fielded for user evaluation in order to strengthen the Army’s combat capability,” sources said. Several contracts for capital acquisitions for the Army were signed during 2016-17. Official sources said 11 contracts were signed with Indian and foreign vendors for ₹12,588.06 crore, for the procurement of various equipment including artillery guns, missiles, rocket launcher system, simulator and ballistic helmets. Acceptance of Necessity (AoN), the very first stage of a military procurement, has also been accorded to eight capital procurement cases for the Army, official sources added, at an estimated cost of ₹19,120.89 crore.

  

**‘Buy Indian’**

  

Of this, four cases are under the ‘Buy Indian’ category at a cost of ₹16,469.14 crore, and two cases are under the ‘Buy (Indian IDDM)’ at a cost of ₹1,684.13 crore. Faced with massive delays in acquiring technologically advanced rifles for its soldiers, “the ministry is to issue tenders for the procurement of the assault rifles and also ink deals on a government to government basis,” sources added.

  

**INSAS Replacement**

  

During the same time, in February 2016, the Alteration Committee of the defence ministry approved modifications in the existing Indian Small Arms System (INSAS) 1B rifle. Sources indicated the INSAS will be replaced with deadlier assault rifles of higher caliber 7.62x51 mm.

  

The assault rifles will be of 7.62 mm calibre, while the carbines will be of 5.56 mm calibre. The request for information (RFI) for the new assault rifle with specification 7.62x51mm has also been issued Sources added that acquisition of new artillery guns, “through five procurement cases that also involve indigenous production,” has also been approved.

  

**Self Propelled Guns**

  

Even as a deal has been signed with the US Government for the procurement of 145 Ultra Light Howitzers (ULH) through the Foreign Military Sale route, a contract has also been signed with Larsen and Toubro for the procurement of 100 self propelled guns.

  

Another indent has also been placed by the defence ministry for the procurement of 114 electronically upgraded gun system from OFB, Kolkata. A case for procurement of 400/1180 Towed Gun System is at the trial stage, as is another case for upgunning of 130 mm guns to 155 mm guns.

The **Excalibur** is an [assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle "Assault rifle") derived from the [INSAS rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INSAS_rifle "INSAS rifle"), the standard rifle of the [Indian Armed Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Armed_Forces "Indian Armed Forces") and, to a lesser extent, the [Indian Police Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Police_Service "Indian Police Service"). The Excalibur has many improvements over the INSAS rifle and was slated to replace it as the [Indian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Army "Indian Army")'s standard assault rifle; however, the Indian Army put the replacement out to tender in September 2016.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-ToI-4) Many police forces in India have procured the Excalibur in limited numbers.

It is manufactured by [Ordnance Factory Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Board "Ordnance Factory Board") in [Rifle Factory Ishapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifle_Factory_Ishapore "Rifle Factory Ishapore").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-5)

The Indian Army used the INSAS rifle from the late 1990s, and the rifle saw action during the [Kargil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kargil_War "Kargil War"). The INSAS was said to be plagued with many reliability issues like cracking of the polymer magazines because of cold weather, oil being sprayed in the user's eyes and the rifle going into automatic mode when set on 3-round burst (the INSAS does not have an automatic mode).

From April 21 to 24, 2008, the Excalibur was shown at the Defence Services Asia convention.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-SAR-6)

In November 2011, the Indian Army sent a [request for proposal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Request_for_proposal "Request for proposal") (RFP) to 34 vendors for 65,678 multi-calibre assault rifles for about [₹](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_rupee "Indian rupee")2,500 [crore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crore "Crore") ([US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")400 million).[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-global-tender-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-five-cos-8) The tender also included a license to manufacture about 100,000 more rifles in India, with a total expenditure of the phasing out estimated at [₹](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_rupee "Indian rupee")5,500 [crore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crore "Crore") ([US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")900 million).[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-butter-9) Similar tenders for a [carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbine "Carbine") and a [light machine gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_machine_gun "Light machine gun") (LMG) were also issued.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-weary-army-10) However, the Army sent a letter to the manufacturers on 15 June 2015, to notify them that the tender had been retracted.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-ScrapTender-11) In July 2015, it was reported that the INSAS may be replaced by the Modified INSAS rifle (MIR), which is based on the Excalibur. The decision was taken by General [Dalbir Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalbir_Singh "Dalbir Singh"), who wanted an indigenous rifle.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-MadeinIndia-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-JanesCancels-13)

After cancelling the tender, the army decided to pursue the new Excalibur rifle developed by the [ARDE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armament_Research_and_Development_Establishment "Armament Research and Development Establishment") as a replacement for the older INSAS rifles.

On 3 July 2016, the Indian media reported that the Indian Army had rejected the Excalibur for its standard issue assault rifle as it did not match the requirements standard of the army.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-ET-14)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-15)

In September 2016 the Indian Army announced that it was launching a tender for 185,000 7.62×51mm-caliber assault rifles.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-ToI-4) The Indian Army in October 2016 announced that Excalibur rifles will be adopted as an interim assault rifle until a suitable replacement is found.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-17)

In June 2017, the Excalibur was announced to have failed tests due to concerns about quality control and ineffective firepower.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-18)

Design of the assault rifle first started in 2004.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-19)

The prototype incorporates a direct gas-tapping angle to reduce the recoil. The rifle would have automatic and single shot modes. The three-round burst mode of the INSAS has been dropped. The rifle would have a folding butt and a standard [Picatinny rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picatinny_rail "Picatinny rail"). By September 2015, it had passed the water and mud tests, which four of the foreign rifles in the tender competition had failed. It was also reported 200 rifles were being manufactured and that prototype would undergo formal trials in late 2015.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-IndigenousExcalibur-20)

The MIR had two stoppages after firing 24,000 rounds, which was very close the army's specification of one stoppage.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-MadeinIndia-12) It was also reported that another prototype of Excalibur, AR-2, was being prepared which would fire 7.62×39mm rounds.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-MadeinIndia-12)

The final designs incorporated picatinny rails on the upper receiver with an improved design for the polycarbonate magazine.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excalibur_rifle#cite_note-JanesCancels-13)

Posted on [August 10, 2016](https://bharatkarnad.com/2016/08/10/ditching-the-excalibur-and-every-other-indigenous-armament/ "2:20 pm") by [Bharat Karnad](https://bharatkarnad.com/author/bharatkarnad/ "View all posts by Bharat Karnad")

The army brass in 2012 decided they wanted a multi-purpose infantry weapon with interchangeable barrels — 5.56x39mm for conventional warfare and the 7.62x51mm for distant kills. Foreign weapons — CM 901 from Colt (US), VZ 58 from Ceska (Czech Republic), possibly SIG 716 or SIG 543 from Sig Sauer (Switzerland), the Israeli possibly Tavor X-95, and the Baretta ARX 160 from Italy — all came up short.

The Excalibur, indigenously designed & developed by the Armaments Research & Development Establishment, Pune and manufactured by the Ordnance Factories Board (OFB), was the Indian entry in this competition. Sure, ‘Excalibur’ is an odd name for an Indian 7.62mm infantry weapon. May be the Ordnance Factory Board hoped that its client, the Indian army leaders, besotted by foreign goods, wouldn’t notice it was not ex-British and would be entranced by the moniker. (Excalibur is the name of the sword stuck in a rock by Merlin, the wizard, that as the legend goes, attracted the young Arthur to pull it out and be crowned King of England — a feat that others failed at, whence Camelot, etc.) And, in any case, it was hoped by OFB that this name would magically win over the army brass who, alas, have proved they are immune to Excalibur’s allurements and appeal. At their annual conference in April 2016, the army commanders decided, in their wisdom or lack thereof that, no matter what, they were done with the Excalibur option and, in the face of the failure of the interchangeable barrels-based concept, that the service would go in for a foreign 7.62mm product as standard infantry weapon.

This despite the proven performance of the Excalibur in field tests in competition with the above-mentioned foreign weapons. A much improved derivative of the INSAS 5.56mm infantry weapon, the Excalibur can be fired in full automatic mode. It failed only twice in repeated and ceaseless firing of some 24,000-odd rounds, a miniscule failure rate level no foreign weapon was able to achieve. Excalibur also fared better in firing after being submerged for long periods of time in muddy water, etc., in other words it did better than any foreign gun in all-weather battlefield conditions the Indian army jawans are most likely to encounter.

But the army commanders, like other military leadership, apparently has a soft corner for “Western maal”. How else to explain their case in support of foreign weapons of 7.76×51 mm calibre that are able to kill an enemy soldier at 500 metres distance, which requirement controverts the modern-era basic logic of infantry weapon?

The whole point about an effective infantry weapon that seems to be lost on the Indian Army’s top leadership echelon is that it should incapacitate an enemy soldier for life, so that he thereafter becomes a social and economic burden for the enemy state to bear. If an enemy soldier is killed outright, there’s only the relatively minimal expense of disposing off the body and pensioning off the spouse. Then there’s the matter of the demoralizing factor — an enemy soldier with a grievous wound being carried away on a stretcher can psychologically unhinge other enemy troops in the vicinity. And there’s the factor of troopers being pulled from the frontlines to carry their injured comrades, thinning out the forward advancing line. This is the logic of the 5.56 mm item as close-in weapon capable of raking fire and gravely incapacitating an enemy at 100 meters, but not of killing fire.

For sure kills at a distance and for sniper missions, the Indian army has always used the Russian Dragunov SVD — derived from indisputably the finest infantry weapon in existence, the Kalashnikov. Had the US Army in the early 1960s the strategic wit to go for the light weight revolutionary plastic-bodied Armalite AR-15 assault rifle (designed by the legendary Eugene Stoner) in Vietnam, who knows, America might have won that war, and the AR-15 would have run the Kalashnikov close for the soldier’s affection worldwide. The US Army chose the heavier M-16 instead, which made a name for itself chiefly for being discarded at the first instance by American troops in the field, who’d pick up the Kalashnikovs from the Viet Cong guerrillas they killed.

So, tell me again, why are our army commanders keen on an imported 7.62??? Surely, not because they are unaware of the 5.56 logic.

But the army commanders’ collective desire has run smack into the defence minister Manohar Parrikar’s dogged insistence on the Indian military going seriously indigenous. So Excalibur is back in the picture, except the senior flagrank types in the army are trying their damndest to somehow kill off this option. Any indigenous armament has to run an obstacle course in MOD and against the armed services. Indeed, Excalibur’s troubles in many ways mirror the problems the Indian designed Arjun MBT is facing with the armoured combat arm. It has beaten every foreign tank, including the Russian T-90S in every field trial and test, and yet it’s being sidelined, and tanks are being imported from Russia. Parrikar is in the right to oppose the French Rafale and to fully support the Tejas Mk-I and Mk-II options. But where the M-777 light mountain gun is concerned, he has erred by preferring it to an equally capable artillery system available in-country.

Parrikar and the Modi government have to decide for once and for all whether they are serious about propelling forward an Indian armament design and development capability, or whether this is just rhetoric the PM can now again wax eloquent with. If the BJP regime is serious then they should institutionally shut down the import route in all its manifestations, and dismantle the military procurement system that, notwithstanding the DPP-2016 still favours the import option under cover of the “MAKE in India” policy. Make in India should be replaced with “MADE in India” and appropriate reforms rung in. But, who wants that?

Of course, getting rid of armament imports will leave a whole bunch of Generals, Air Marshals, Admirals, and officers downstream in the acquisitions loop crying in their cups — because they will be suddenly denied foreign trips, padded accounts, and scholarships for progeny, rich post-retirement jobs offered by Indian companies fronting for foreign suppliers, etc., which benefits political leaders and senior bureaucrats have availed of from the early days of the republic. But the military is catching up fast on this corruption front! (The eye-popping extent and scale of corruption in the Indian armed forces to match the extant corruption in the civilian quarters of the Indian government, is revealed in Josy Joseph’s book — A Feast of Vultures: The Hidden Business of Democracy in India.)

Excalibur rifle awaits certification trials
===========================================

Excalibur, a fully automatic rifle that fires 5.56mm ammunition, is an upgraded version of INSAS rifle, which was inducted in the mid-nineties.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Updated \- July 07, 2016 12:19 pm IST - NEW DELHI:

[Dinakar Peri](https://www.thehindu.com/profile/author/Dinakar-Peri/)

READ LATER

[SEE ALL](https://www.thehindu.com/myaccount/?tab=bookmarks) Remove

[![Image 10: Google Preferred Source](https://www.thehindu.com/theme/images/th-online/google-preferred-badge.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=https://www.thehindu.com/)

![Image 11](https://www.thehindu.com/theme/images/th-online/1x1_spacer.png)

An indigenously produced new generation rifle, Excalibur, is awaiting user trials and final certification, even as the Army seems to be moving away to a bigger calibre rifle than what has been produced by the Ordnance Factory Board (OFB).

“Fifteen rifles are ready at the Rifle Factory, Ishapore, for user and Director General Quality Assurance evaluation and awaiting trail directive from the Infantry Directorate,” OFB spokesperson told _The Hindu_ .

The Excalibur is a fully automatic rifle which fires 5.56mm ammunition and is an upgraded version of the current INSAS (Indian National Small Arms System) which was inducted in the mid-nineties but had a troubled history all along.

The Rifle Factory, Ishapore has produced 15 prototypes with modifications based on user feedback on reliability, weight, length, compatibility with international sights, aesthetics etc. and has been evaluated by users at the Army’s Infantry School at Mhow, OFB officials said.

“User has recently asked for a few additional features to be incorporated in the rifle. OFB has assured introduction of proposed balance four modifications in a time-bound manner,” the spokesperson said, adding that the project was a joint effort of the OFB and Infantry Directorate.

The Army has been attempting to procure a new standard issue rifle for a decade. Recently, the overambitious tender for rifles with interchangeable barrels was cancelled after a four year process as no vendor could meet the requirements. After that, the Army decided to go for 7.62mm calibre and new Staff Quality Requirements are being drawn up.

Army officials said that due this decision, Excalibur is unlikely to be adopted as the standard issue in the current form but stated that its user trials and the process for a new rifle would continue simultaneously.

There are a large number of INSAS guns which need replacement and repairs. They need to be maintained till the new process is completed. So Excalibur can be certified and used to replace the INSAS till the new rifles are procured,” a senior officer observed.

It is very hard to do a before/after analysis because other variables also changes over time (for example, violence went up 93-96, 00-03, 16-20; dipped in intervening years). > ramana wrote:Is it 9mm? Then its Sterling replacement. Correct assessment.

But no one wants a Sterling replacement: carrying one during IPKF and early days of the Kashmir Insurgency was a "shoot me first -- I'm an officer or radio operator" advertisement for enemies. The 9x19mm bullets couldn't penetrate even the light cover. That (along with Sterling open-bolt action problems) was one of the big reasons most YOs hated SMGs, and took on captured or newly bought AKMs as soon as possible.  
  
At best, this is an indigenous substitution to the limited number of B&T MP9s that Ghatak-platoon scouts use (usually with suppressors to kill enemy guards and dogs). AKM is still preferred. Outside of the army, of course, it has plenty of applications for police and paramilitary forces.
